title: Technology Is Not the Treatment: A Pragmatic Clinical Reasoning Guide for Technology-Enhanced Rehabilitation
content: Rehabilitation technologies can create opportunities for feedback, assistance, adjustable practice, and interaction that are difficult to reproduce in some clinical settings. Yet an engaging device or a sophisticated interface does not, by itself, establish a reason to use it with a particular patient. Clinicians often encounter a practical question before adopting an exergame, an extended-reality system, interactive biofeedback, or a robotic device: what would this technology contribute to the treatment that a reasonable alternative would not? Existing frameworks address treatment specification, gaming-based rehabilitation, device matching, and technology adoption. Building on these contributions, this Perspective proposes Technology-Enhanced Rehabilitation (TER) as a brief, non-prescriptive clinical reasoning guide organized around four questions: What does the patient need to change? What relevant contribution might the technology add compared with a reasonable alternative? Is that contribution worthwhile and feasible for this patient and context? Is the expected value being realized? A hypothetical case involving return to recreational football after persistent knee pain illustrates decisions to use, trial, adapt, or forgo an exergame. The proposal does not assert that interactive technologies are superior to conventional rehabilitation, introduce new treatment mechanisms, or offer validated decision rules. Its purpose is to make the rationale for choosing—and choosing not to use—technology explicit, clinically discussable, and open to future evaluation.
